title: Cut-Paper Manifesto — Design Graduate Portfolio Cover
description: A bold portfolio cover that stacks a towering display name over a cut-paper self-portrait, with rotated discipline stickers and contact info anchored to the lower margin. Marigold ground, cobalt, and hot-pink accents telegraph art-school energy without filtering it.
philosophy: This template exists to announce rather than introduce — built for the graduate who has earned the right to take up space. It refuses the restrained minimalism of corporate portfolio decks, borrowing instead from zine culture, hand-torn paper, and type posters where nothing whispers. The grid is a suggestion: sticker tags rotate freely, the portrait bleeds, and the name demands to be read from across the room. Its natural habitat is the graduate-show wall and the hiring director who has already seen a hundred tidy, forgettable PDFs.
goodFor: Design-school graduate show opening title slides
Personal portfolio covers where name recognition and personality are the primary goal
Art-direction or illustration portfolios with a strong handmade visual identity
Printed broadsheet or physical portfolio book covers
avoidFor: Client-facing pitch decks requiring brand restraint and visual consistency
Chart-heavy quarterly business reviews or data presentations
Multi-slide decks that need a repeatable, structured interior layout
Academic research presentations with dense body text
author: harness

examples.promptCore: This slide is a manifesto cover, not an introduction — it draws from zine culture, hand-torn paper ephemera, and oversized type posters where the name is the loudest object in the room. The composition is deliberately asymmetric and layered: collage textures overlap, sticker fragments rotate against the grain, and the portrait sits mid-collision with the title stack. The mood is art-school urgency — raw, physical, unapologetically loud. Avoid visual quietude, centered symmetry, or corporate polish; if it could appear on a restrained PDF template, it does not belong here.

examples.layoutNotes: Full-bleed ground with no outer margin restraint; the display name stacks in two to three oversized lines anchored upper-left, deliberately spilling past the column guides to claim edge-to-edge presence. A cut-paper portrait graphic occupies the lower-center zone, layered beneath the type stack and bleeding off the bottom edge entirely. Three to five sticker-tag elements rotate freely between −20° and +20° across the mid-field, obeying no column alignment. Contact line and discipline label sit flush-left at the bottom, hugging the lower 8% margin as the sole anchored footer element.

examples.promptCore: The slide should read like a page torn straight from a graduate-show manifesto zine — layered paper shapes, rotated annotation tags, and raw collage texture doing the hierarchical work that white space would handle in a restrained system. Compositional rhythm is deliberately asymmetric: a rough paper-backed content card anchors one quadrant while sticker satellites create visual tension around it, giving the eye multiple entry points without a single obvious reading order. The mood is urgent and handmade, closer to a bulletin board arranged with conviction than a designed layout. Avoid any centered symmetry, airy margins, or compositional cues that suggest corporate tidiness or academic neutrality.

examples.layoutNotes: 12-column soft grid; the primary content block — a stat callout, manifesto quote, or sticker-tagged feature cluster — occupies cols 2–9 on a torn-paper card shape that bleeds ~10% past the left column boundary. Two to four rotated sticker-tag labels (±6–14°) orbit the card as satellites, landing in the upper-right corner zone and lower-left margin. Page folio anchors the lower-right outside the collision zone; no header band — the stacked visual mass replaces it. Outer margin is compressed (~5%) to reinforce wall-poster density over document breathing room.
